India's sharp fall in extreme poverty as global progress slows

TOI Data Desk

India has sharply reduced extreme poverty, but the global fight is losing momentum. Explore what three poverty lines reveal about India's states, its neighbours and the wider world.

India

Same survey, same year, three answers

The World Bank uses three daily poverty lines per person: $3 measures extreme poverty; $4.20 and $8.30 reflect poverty standards in lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries.

The amounts are adjusted for what money can buy in different countries. Switch the line to see how India’s 2023–24 survey tells three different stories.

At $4.20 a day, the World Bank estimates that 49.6 crore fewer Indians were below the line in 2023–24 than in 2011–12.

    Who remains

    Who is still below the line

    At the $4.20 line, about 22 in every 100 children live in poor households, compared with about 14 in every 100 working-age adults. Poverty is also more common in rural areas and among people with little schooling.

    Below $4.20 a day · 2023–24 · Schooling: ages 16 and above. These rates reflect household consumption per person.

    China and India, side by side

    The higher the threshold, the wider the gap. India’s figures are from 2023–24; China’s are from 2022.

    The displayed China $3 rate of 0.0% is rounded, not a claim that nobody is poor.

    The World Bank says China went from roughly a billion people in extreme poverty in 1990 to almost none by 2015. India’s decline accelerated later. Together, they account for much of the global fall.

    The billions between the two lines

    About 2.9 billion people, or 36 in every 100 worldwide, lived above $3 but below $8.30 a day in 2024. Escaping extreme poverty is not the same as reaching financial security.

    For 2026, the World Bank projects 811 million people below $3 and about 3.7 billion below $8.30.

    Why is global progress slowing?

    Rapid growth in Asia drove much of the earlier fall. With extreme poverty now low in many of those economies, further gains depend increasingly on countries held back by weak growth, too few productive jobs, conflict and fragility.

    The World Bank’s October 2026 report says nine economies account for more than half of the world’s extremely poor. By 2030, it projects that 87% will live in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile or conflict-affected countries, or both.

    A separate May 2026 World Bank analysis found that, over the preceding decade, extreme poverty rose in Nigeria, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Pakistan and Sudan. It fell modestly in DR Congo and Tanzania, and sharply in India.

    What could change

    More people working. And better pay for their work.

    The World Bank modelled how wider employment and better earning power could reduce extreme poverty worldwide.

    More people in work
    ~20%
    less extreme poverty worldwide

    If three in four working-age adults in poor households had work (75% employment).

    Better earning power
    Nearly 50%
    less extreme poverty worldwide

    If poor workers had the same average level of schooling as people above the extreme-poverty line. The model predicts earnings about 40% higher.

    The bigger picture

    Poverty has fallen. Prosperity is another question.

    2.6%$3 a day
    80.0%$8.30 a day

    India has made major progress against extreme poverty. But the higher poverty lines show how far living standards still have to rise.

    The World Bank says further progress will increasingly depend on creating productive employment in the states where poverty remains concentrated.
